C1.1: No terms of reference for an HSE Steering Committee were available, and the contractor could not show that a committee had been formally established for the project. Without a steering committee there is no structured forum for senior management to review HSE performance and direct resources.

An HSE Steering Committee had been established on paper, but the attendance records showed that neither the PD nor the CEO had attended any of the recent meetings. Senior management representation is a requirement, and meetings chaired only by HSE personnel do not demonstrate leadership commitment.

The steering committee membership list did not include the construction manager or any operational leaders, and was limited to HSE staff and an administrator. The committee therefore lacked the authority to assign actions to the people who control site activities.

The steering committee terms of reference stated a monthly frequency, yet records showed that meetings had lapsed for several consecutive months. The contractor must reinstate the agreed frequency and demonstrate senior management attendance at each meeting.

Senior management were named as committee members, but they were repeatedly represented by delegates with no decision-making authority. Delegation at this level undermines the purpose of the committee and should be limited to exceptional cases with a documented reason.

Main subcontractors carrying significant high-risk scopes were not represented on the HSE Steering Committee. Their exclusion means subcontractor HSE performance, resourcing and repeated findings were not reviewed at senior level, and the membership should be revised accordingly.
C1.2: The contractor could not provide any record of actions raised during the most recent senior management walkthrough. A walkthrough without documented observations and assigned actions provides no evidence of leadership intervention and cannot be followed up.

Actions were recorded from the senior management walkthrough, but they had no owners or target dates and several remained open well beyond a reasonable closure period. The contractor must track walkthrough actions in a register and verify closure with evidence.

The walkthrough report contained only general comments on housekeeping and did not address the high-risk activities ongoing at the time, such as work at height and lifting operations. Senior management walkthroughs should focus on critical controls and significant hazards.

Walkthrough actions were marked as closed in the tracker, yet the same unsafe conditions were found on site during the audit. Closure had been accepted without photographic or physical verification, which indicates that the close-out process is ineffective.

There was no evidence that senior management engaged with frontline workers or supervisors during the walkthrough, as no conversations, observations or feedback were recorded. Visible felt leadership requires direct interaction with the workforce and not only a site inspection.

The outcomes of the senior management walkthrough were not communicated to the workforce through toolbox talks or presented at the steering committee. Findings that are not shared or reviewed do not drive improvement across the project.
C1.3: Minutes for the most recent HSE Steering Committee were not available at the time of the audit, and the contractor stated they were still being drafted. Minutes must be issued promptly so that agreed actions can be tracked and verified.

The latest steering committee minutes were available but did not include any review of injuries or illnesses recorded during the reporting period. Incident performance is a mandatory agenda item, and its omission means trends and root causes were not discussed by senior management.

The minutes made no reference to HIPO near misses, although the incident register showed that HIPO events had been reported during the same period. High-potential events must be reviewed at steering committee level to confirm that lessons learned and controls are in place.

HIPO unsafe behaviours and conditions were not discussed in the steering committee, and the minutes covered only statistics and upcoming activities. The agenda should be revised to include a structured review of high-potential observations and the effectiveness of corrective actions.

The minutes recorded discussion topics but contained no action log with owners and due dates, and actions from the previous meeting were not reviewed. Without action tracking, the committee cannot demonstrate that decisions were implemented.

The steering committee minutes were generic and appeared to be copied from the previous meeting with only figures updated. The content did not reflect current project risks or recent incidents, which indicates that meaningful review had not taken place.
C1.4: No HSE audit schedule was available for the current period, and the contractor could not demonstrate a planned programme of internal audits. Audits were being carried out reactively, which does not meet the requirement for systematic verification of the HSE management system.

An audit schedule existed, but the planned audits for recent months had not been conducted and no revised dates had been recorded. Missed audits leave compliance gaps undetected, and the schedule must be recovered with evidence of completion.

A recent internal audit report was available; however, there was no evidence that it had been reviewed by senior management or presented at the steering committee. Audit findings that do not reach senior management are unlikely to receive the resources needed for closure.

The audit schedule did not include subcontractor audits, although several subcontractors were performing high-risk scopes on site. The contractor must extend the audit programme to cover all subcontractors in line with their risk profile.

Findings from the most recent audit were recorded, but no corrective action plan had been developed and several findings were repeated from the previous audit. Repeated findings indicate that the audit outcomes are not being acted upon.

The audit report reviewed did not identify the auditor or confirm the auditor's competence, and the scope was limited to document checks without site verification. Audits must be conducted by competent personnel and include field verification of implementation.
C1.5: No schedule for senior management HSE engagement was available, and the contractor could not show planned dates for PD or CEO participation in site walkthroughs. Leadership engagement was occurring on an ad hoc basis without a defined programme.

A senior management schedule was provided, but it covered only meetings and did not include participation in HSE walkthroughs. The schedule must be revised to include planned site walkthroughs by the PD and CEO at the required frequency.

The walkthrough schedule listed the PD and CEO, but records showed that planned walkthroughs had been missed or cancelled without rescheduling. The contractor must track compliance against the schedule and report it to the steering committee.

The senior management schedule was out of date and referred to a previous project phase, and it did not reflect the current work fronts or high-risk activities. An outdated schedule cannot direct leadership attention to where current risks exist.

Walkthroughs recorded against the senior management schedule were attended only by HSE representatives on behalf of the PD and CEO. Delegated attendance does not satisfy the requirement for visible senior leadership participation on site.

The schedule did not cover night shift operations, although significant activities were being performed at night. Senior management walkthroughs should be planned across all shifts so that leadership is visible to the entire workforce.
C1.6: The contractor could not provide the NCs, opportunities for improvement or corrective action recommendations raised in the most recent audit. Without a record of audit outcomes, the effectiveness of the audit process could not be verified.

Audit nonconformities were listed, but no corrective actions had been proposed and no responsible persons or target dates had been assigned. The contractor must develop a corrective action plan for each NC and track it to closure.

Corrective actions recommended by the auditor addressed only the immediate symptoms and did not identify root causes. Actions such as reissuing a reminder or retraining an individual are unlikely to prevent recurrence of systemic failures.

Several NCs raised in the previous audit were found to be repeated during this audit, although they had been recorded as closed. Closure had been accepted without adequate verification, which indicates weaknesses in the close-out process.

Opportunities for improvement raised by the auditor had not been reviewed or responded to, and there was no record of whether they had been accepted or rejected. All audit outputs should be formally reviewed and their status recorded.

The audit NC register was maintained by the HSE department only, and there was no evidence that it had been shared with the construction team responsible for the findings. Ownership of corrective actions must sit with the operational managers who control the work.
C1.7: No schedule for mass toolbox talks was available, and the contractor stated that mass TBTs were organised only after incidents. A planned schedule is required so that key messages and campaigns are delivered to the whole workforce at a regular frequency.

A mass TBT schedule was available, but it did not include participation by the external PD or CEO. Senior management attendance at mass TBTs is required to demonstrate visible leadership commitment to the workforce.

The mass TBT schedule showed participation by senior management, but attendance records and photographs indicated that they had not attended the recent sessions. The contractor must verify and record actual senior management participation against the schedule.

Mass TBTs were delivered in English only, while a large part of the workforce did not understand English, and no translation arrangements were evident. Messages that are not understood by the workforce do not achieve the intended outcome.

The mass TBT topics were generic and repeated across sessions, and they did not reflect recent incidents, HIPO events or upcoming high-risk activities. Topics should be selected based on current risks and lessons learned on the project.

The mass TBT schedule did not include subcontractor workforce or night shift personnel, and attendance sheets confirmed that these groups were not present. All personnel on site must be included in mass TBTs, either through combined or repeated sessions.
C1.8: No evidence of recognition or reward for frontline workers reporting high-potential near misses was available. The contractor could not show that reporting of critical control failures was being encouraged, which may contribute to under-reporting.

A recognition programme existed, but awards had been given only for general good housekeeping and attendance, and none related to HIPO near miss reporting or critical controls. The criteria should be revised to reward reporting of significant hazards.

Recognition records showed that rewards were given mainly to supervisors and HSE staff rather than frontline workers. The scheme must prioritise workers who report high-potential observations, as they are closest to the hazards.

The recognition programme had not been implemented for several months, and no rewards had been issued during the period although HIPO observations had been reported. A scheme that is not applied consistently loses credibility with the workforce.

Recognised observations were not communicated to the wider workforce through toolbox talks, notice boards or mass TBTs. Publicising recognition is an important part of reinforcing positive reporting behaviour and should be included in the programme.

There was no defined selection process for recognising HIPO reports, and awards appeared to be chosen informally without reference to the observation register. The contractor must establish transparent criteria linked to the quality and potential severity of each report.
C1.9: Work was found in progress on site under a RAMS that had not yet been approved and was still under review on Aconex. Managers and supervisors must ensure that no activity starts until its RAMS has received the required approval.

The RAMS for the activity had been approved, but the supervisor could not demonstrate that it had been briefed to the work crew, and no briefing attendance record was available. Approved controls that are not communicated cannot be implemented.

The supervisor did not understand English, and the RAMS had not been translated into a language understood by the supervisor or the workers. No evidence was provided that the pre-task briefing had been properly translated for the crew.

Controls specified in the approved RAMS were not implemented at the work location, including barricading and the designated exclusion zone. Supervisors had not verified that the RAMS requirements were in place before work commenced.

The work crew had changed since the RAMS briefing, and new workers had joined the activity without being briefed on the method statement and risk assessment. A re-briefing must be conducted and recorded whenever crew members change.

Supervisors were using a RAMS that had been approved with Code B comments, and the comments had not been incorporated before work started. The contractor must ensure that all Code B comments are closed and communicated before the RAMS is used on site.
C1.10: A RAMS register was available, but sampling of activities on site identified work being performed without a corresponding RAMS listed in the register. All activities must be covered by an approved RAMS before work begins.

The RAMS for the sampled activity was not accessible on site, and no hard copy was available at the work location. The crew and supervisor were therefore unable to refer to the approved method and controls during the work.

The RAMS register had not been updated, and it did not reflect the current revision or approval code of several documents on Aconex. An inaccurate register prevents supervisors from confirming that they are working to the latest approved RAMS.

The copy of the RAMS kept on site was a superseded revision, while a later revision with additional controls had been approved. Superseded documents must be withdrawn from site and replaced with the current approved revision.

No RAMS register was maintained for subcontractor activities, and subcontractor crews could not produce their RAMS at the work location. The contractor must include subcontractor RAMS in the register and ensure copies are available on site.

The RAMS register listed documents as approved, but several were recorded on Aconex with Code C status and had not been resubmitted. Activities covered by rejected RAMS must not proceed until a revised document receives Code A or Code B approval.
C1.11: The RAMS sampled was generic and described a broader scope, and it did not cover the specific activity being performed at the work location. RAMS must be activity-specific so that the hazards and controls reflect the actual work.

The risk assessment did not identify all relevant significant hazards, and hazards such as working near live services and simultaneous operations were omitted. Unidentified hazards are not controlled, and the RAMS must be revised.

The RAMS described the required controls, but several mandated controls were not in place on site, including edge protection and the specified permit. The gap between the documented method and site practice must be closed before work continues.

The method statement sequence did not match the way the work was being carried out, and the crew had adopted a different method without a formal change. Any change to the method requires a revised RAMS and reassessment of the risks.

The plant and equipment listed in the RAMS differed from the equipment in use on site, and the hazards associated with the substituted equipment had not been assessed. The RAMS must reflect the actual plant used.

The RAMS did not specify the competency or certification required for key roles, and personnel performing the activity did not hold the training referenced in the risk assessment. Competence requirements must be clearly defined and verified before work starts.
C1.12: No documented procedure for the review and approval of RAMS was available, and the contractor relied on informal practice. A defined review process is required to ensure consistency and that each RAMS is checked by competent personnel.

RAMS were being submitted to the Employer without internal review or signature by the construction manager. Authorisation by the relevant construction manager is required to confirm that the method is practicable and resourced.

The review process did not define when a RAMS must be revised, and several documents had not been reviewed despite changes in scope, equipment or site conditions. Triggers for review must be documented and applied.

RAMS reviewed by the Employer with Code B comments were being used without evidence that the comments had been addressed and the revised document resubmitted on Aconex. The process must ensure that comments are closed within the required timeframe.

The RAMS review process did not include participation by the supervisors and workers who would perform the activity. Involving the work crew in the review improves the identification of practical hazards and should be built into the process.

Subcontractor RAMS were forwarded directly to the Employer without review or endorsement by the main contractor. The main contractor remains responsible for all RAMS on its scope and must review and authorise subcontractor submissions before submittal.
C2.2: The HSSE plan available on site was still under review on Aconex and had not achieved Code A approval from the Employer. Work had progressed without an approved HSSE plan, which is the primary document governing HSE management on the project.

The HSSE plan was returned by the Employer with Code B comments, and the comments had not been incorporated or resubmitted. The contractor must close all outstanding comments and obtain Code A approval without further delay.

The approved HSSE plan was an outdated revision and did not reflect the current scope of work, organisation structure or manpower. The plan must be revised and resubmitted whenever there are significant changes to the project.

Updates shown during the audit, including new KPIs and objectives, were not included in the approved HSSE plan. Changes to the plan must be formally submitted on Aconex and approved before they replace the approved content.

The HSSE plan had been approved, but several of its commitments were not implemented on site, including the inspection frequencies and the reward and recognition programme. An approved plan must be reflected in actual site practice.

The HSSE plan had not been communicated to supervisors and key personnel, and several supervisors were unaware of the roles and responsibilities assigned to them. The plan must be briefed to all relevant personnel with records maintained.
C2.3: No HSSE monitoring schedule had been submitted to the Employer, and inspections and audits were conducted without a defined plan. A monitoring schedule is required to ensure that all workplaces, equipment and activities are checked at the required frequency.
The HSSE monitoring schedule was returned with Code C status and had not been revised and resubmitted on Aconex. The contractor was therefore operating without an approved monitoring programme.

The approved monitoring schedule was outdated and did not include recently started activities such as steel erection and confined space work. The schedule must be updated as the project progresses so that all high-risk activities are monitored.

Inspections and audits listed in the approved monitoring schedule had not been carried out at the stated frequency, and several planned inspections had no records. The contractor must demonstrate compliance with the schedule it has committed to.

The monitoring schedule did not assign responsibilities, and there was no evidence that supervisors or HSE officers were aware of the inspections they were expected to perform. Each monitoring activity must have a named role responsible for completion.

The monitoring schedule had been approved with Code B comments requiring the addition of subcontractor monitoring, but the comments had not been closed. Subcontractor activities remained outside the monitoring programme.
C2.4: The training matrix had not been submitted for Employer approval, and the training plan available on site was an internal draft. Without an approved training matrix there is no agreed baseline for the mandatory training required for each role.

The training matrix was approved, but training records showed that several personnel had not completed the mandatory courses listed for their roles. The contractor must close training gaps and maintain a tracker to monitor compliance.

The training needs analysis did not include mandatory training for construction leaders, such as risk assessment and permit-to-work training for supervisors. The matrix must be revised to cover all roles, including management and supervisory positions.

The induction presentation in use had not been approved by the Employer and did not include current site emergency contact numbers and project-specific rules. An approved, up-to-date induction is required for all personnel before they start work.

Training was delivered by personnel who could not demonstrate competence in the subject, and no train-the-trainer certificate or equivalent qualification was available. Trainers must be competent and their qualifications recorded in the training records.

Training records showed that refresher induction had not been carried out for long-serving personnel, although the approved training plan required periodic refreshers. Overdue refreshers must be scheduled and completed.
C2.5: CVs for several HSSE personnel deployed on site had not been submitted to the Employer for approval. Personnel must not be appointed to HSSE positions until their CVs have been approved on Aconex.

The CV of the HSE manager was returned with Code C status, but the individual continued to perform the role on site. The contractor must replace the individual or obtain approval of a suitable candidate.

Approved CVs did not match the HSSE organisation chart, and some positions in the chart were filled by personnel whose approval had been granted for a different role. Approval is role-specific and must be obtained for the position actually held.

The approved CV register was not maintained, and the contractor could not readily demonstrate the approval status of each HSSE staff member. A register linked to Aconex submittals should be kept up to date.

HSSE personnel CVs had been approved, but the supporting certificates referenced in the CVs had expired and had not been renewed. The contractor must ensure that qualifications remain valid for the duration of the appointment.

The HSSE staffing level did not meet the ratio required by NEOM standards for the current manpower, and replacement personnel had not yet been submitted for approval. The contractor must mobilise sufficient approved HSSE personnel.
C2.6: No HSSE reward and recognition scheme had been submitted for Employer approval, and recognition on site was informal. A formal scheme with defined criteria is required to encourage safe behaviour and reporting.

The reward and recognition scheme was not reflected in the current approved HSSE plan, and the contractor was applying criteria that had not been agreed with the Employer. The scheme must be incorporated into the plan and approved.

The scheme was approved, but there was no evidence that rewards had been issued during recent months. An approved scheme that is not implemented does not motivate the workforce and indicates a lack of management follow-through.

The approved scheme did not define clear selection criteria, and the nominations reviewed appeared to be based on supervisor preference rather than documented observations. Transparent criteria linked to HSE performance must be applied.

The reward and recognition scheme had been approved with Code B comments requiring the inclusion of subcontractor workforce, and the comments had not been addressed. Subcontractor workers remained excluded from recognition.

The scheme focused only on lagging indicators such as days without injury, which may discourage the reporting of incidents. The scheme should be revised to reward proactive behaviours such as near miss reporting and stop-work interventions.
C2.7: The emergency management and emergency response plan had not been submitted to the Employer for approval, and the contractor was using a generic corporate procedure. A project-specific approved plan is required that reflects site layout, resources and NEOM emergency arrangements.

The emergency response plan contained outdated emergency contact numbers, and the old emergency number was still displayed on notice boards and helmet stickers. All references must be updated to the current NEOM emergency contact number.

The approved emergency response plan did not cover current high-risk scenarios such as rescue from height and confined space emergencies. Specific rescue arrangements must be developed for these activities and included in the plan.

Emergency drills required by the approved plan had not been conducted at the stated frequency, and no drill reports or lessons learned were available. The contractor must conduct drills and record their outcomes.

The emergency response plan was returned with Code B comments, and the comments on muster points and emergency team appointments had not been closed. The plan must be revised and resubmitted for Code A approval.

Members of the emergency response team listed in the plan were not aware of their roles, and some had demobilised from the project. The emergency team must be kept current, trained, and briefed on their responsibilities.
C2.8: No injury and illness management plan had been submitted to the Employer for approval. The contractor could not demonstrate defined arrangements for first aid, medical treatment, case management and return to work.

The approved injury and illness management plan did not reflect the current manpower, and medical staffing on site did not meet NEOM requirements for the workforce size. The plan and medical resources must be updated to match current manpower.

The plan was returned with Code C status and had not been resubmitted on Aconex, yet the contractor was operating on the basis of the rejected document. A revised plan must be submitted and approved without delay.

The injury and illness management plan did not include heat stress illness management and medical surveillance, although work was being performed in high ambient temperatures. These arrangements must be added and implemented.

Medical treatment cases had been managed on site, but the case management and reporting process required by the approved plan had not been followed. Cases were not classified or reported to the Employer within the required timeframe.

The approved plan required a medical emergency evacuation procedure, but the ambulance arrangements and transfer route to the nearest medical facility were not established on site. The contractor must verify that medical evacuation can be carried out as planned.
C2.9: The subcontractor management plan had not been updated since the start of the project, and it did not reflect the subcontractors currently mobilised. The plan must be revised to cover all current subcontractors and their scopes.

The subcontractor management plan did not include the pre-qualification process, pre-mobilisation requirements or evaluation scheme. These elements are essential to ensure that only competent subcontractors are mobilised and their performance is monitored.

Subcontractor monthly evaluations required by the approved plan were carried out, but the evaluation report recorded one of the subcontractor's active scopes as not applicable. The evaluation process must assess every scope that the subcontractor performs.
The plan was approved with Code B comments, and the comments relating to subcontractor HSE resourcing had not been incorporated. The revised plan must be resubmitted on Aconex for Code A approval.

A subcontractor had been mobilised to site without completing the pre-mobilisation review required by the approved plan, and its RAMS and HSE personnel had not been approved. The contractor must not allow subcontractors to start work until all mobilisation requirements are met.

The subcontractor management plan had not been communicated to subcontractor management, and subcontractor supervisors were unaware of the reporting and inspection requirements. The plan must be briefed and acknowledged by each subcontractor.
C2.10: The traffic management and logistics plan had not been submitted for Employer approval, and vehicle movements on site were uncontrolled. An approved plan is required to separate pedestrians and vehicles and manage logistics traffic.

The main access roads were congested during peak hours, with water tankers, diesel bowsers, buses and plant moving simultaneously, and there was no pedestrian walkway. Man-machine interface observations were witnessed, which indicates that the plan was not implemented.

The approved traffic management plan was outdated and did not reflect the current site layout, new access routes or laydown areas. The plan and associated traffic drawings must be revised and resubmitted as the site configuration changes.

Traffic management controls specified in the approved plan, including banksmen at reversing points, speed limit signage and segregation barriers, were not in place at several locations. The contractor must implement the controls as approved.

The traffic management plan was returned with Code B comments on delivery scheduling and night-time movements, and these had not been closed. The contractor must address the comments and obtain Code A approval.

Drivers and plant operators had not been briefed on the traffic management plan, and several could not describe the designated routes or speed limits. The plan must be communicated to all drivers, including delivery drivers from suppliers.
C2.11: The lifting operations management plan had not been submitted to the Employer for approval, and lifting operations were taking place without an approved framework. An approved plan is required that defines lift categories, competencies and responsibilities.

A crane lift was in progress without a lift plan available at the work location, and the operator and rigger could not confirm the load weight or radius. Every lift must be planned and the lift plan must be available on site.

The lift plan available did not match the crane in use, as a different crane model with a different load chart had been mobilised. The lift plan must be revised whenever the equipment or configuration changes.

The approved lifting operations management plan required an appointed person to approve critical lifts, but no appointment letter or competency evidence was available. The contractor must formally appoint competent personnel for lift planning and supervision.

The lifting operations management plan was approved with Code B comments on tandem and critical lifts, and the comments had not been addressed. Critical lifts must not proceed until the revised plan has been approved.

Lift plans had been prepared, but they were not briefed to the lifting crew, and no signatures or briefing records were available. The crew must be briefed on the lift plan before each lift and the briefing recorded.
C2.12: No fatigue management plan had been submitted for Employer approval, and the contractor could not demonstrate controls on working hours or rest periods. Fatigue is a significant risk given the extended shifts on the project.

Timesheets reviewed showed that several workers and operators had worked hours exceeding the limits defined in the approved fatigue management plan. The plan was not being implemented and working hours must be monitored and controlled.

The approved fatigue management plan did not address night shift work, long-distance commuting between accommodation and site, or rest breaks during high temperatures. These factors contribute to fatigue on the project and must be included.
The fatigue management plan was returned with Code C status, and no revised plan had been submitted on Aconex. The contractor was operating without an approved fatigue management arrangement.

Supervisors were not aware of the fatigue management plan, and there was no process for identifying or reporting fatigued workers at the start of shift. The plan must be briefed to supervisors with clear fit-for-work checks.

The plan required monitoring of driver and plant operator hours, but no records of driving hours were maintained. Professional drivers and operators must have their hours tracked against the approved limits.
C2.13: The fire prevention plan had not been submitted to the Employer for approval, and fire risks on site were managed without a documented plan. An approved plan is required that covers fire risk assessment, hot work control and firefighting equipment.
The approved fire prevention plan was outdated and did not include the fuel storage area and new fabrication workshop. The plan must be updated whenever new fire risks are introduced on site.

Fire extinguishers at several locations were missing, discharged or past their inspection date, contrary to the requirements of the approved fire prevention plan. Firefighting equipment must be inspected and maintained as specified.

The plan required fire watchers for all hot work, but welding and cutting activities were observed without a fire watcher or fire blanket. The hot work controls defined in the plan were not implemented.

The fire prevention plan was approved with Code B comments relating to the storage of flammable materials, and the comments had not been closed. Flammable materials were found stored close to ignition sources.
Fire wardens named in the fire prevention plan had not received fire warden training, and several had left the project. The fire warden list must be updated and appointed personnel trained.
C2.14: The temporary electrical management safety plan had not been submitted for Employer approval. Temporary electrical installations were being installed and maintained without an approved framework for design, inspection and isolation.

The plan required a competent electrical engineer to be appointed, but there was no formal letter of appointment confirming responsibility for temporary electrical installations and inspections. The appointment must be formalised by the project manager.

Electrical distribution boards were found without RCD protection and were not locked, contrary to the approved temporary electrical plan. The contractor must inspect all temporary installations and correct the deficiencies.

The inspection and testing frequencies defined in the approved plan were not being followed, and several distribution boards had no inspection tags or records. Periodic inspection must be carried out and recorded as required.

The temporary electrical management safety plan was returned with Code B comments on lockout-tagout and generator earthing, and these had not been addressed. The plan must be revised and resubmitted for Code A approval.

The approved temporary electrical plan was outdated and did not include the temporary power supply arrangements for the new work areas. The plan and single line diagrams must be updated to reflect the current installations.
C2.15: Testing and commissioning activities had commenced, but no testing and commissioning plan had been submitted to the Employer for approval. An approved plan is required to manage energisation, pressure testing and handover risks.

The testing and commissioning plan did not include the isolation and permit arrangements for energising systems, and it did not define the interface with the permit-to-work system. These controls are essential to prevent accidental energisation.

The plan was returned with Code C status and had not been resubmitted on Aconex, although pre-commissioning tests were in progress. Testing activities must not continue until an approved plan is in place.

The approved testing and commissioning plan required exclusion zones during pressure testing, but no barricades or warning signs were in place at the test location. The plan must be implemented as approved.

The testing and commissioning plan was not current, as it referred only to mechanical systems and did not cover electrical and fire protection system testing now in progress. The plan must be updated to cover all systems being commissioned.

Personnel performing testing activities had not been briefed on the commissioning plan, and no competency records were available for the commissioning engineers. The contractor must verify competence and brief the plan to all involved.
C2.16: No temporary works procedure or register had been submitted for Employer approval, and temporary works such as formwork, falsework and excavation support were not being controlled. An approved procedure is required to ensure designs are checked and permits issued.

A temporary works register was available but had not been updated, and several temporary works structures on site were not listed. The register must include all temporary works with their design status and inspection records.

The approved procedure required the appointment of a temporary works coordinator, but no coordinator had been appointed and there was no evidence of design checks. The contractor must appoint a competent coordinator.

Temporary works structures were loaded without a permit to load as required by the approved procedure, and no inspection record had been completed before use. Permits to load and strike must be implemented.
The temporary works management plan was approved with Code B comments on the design check categories, and the comments had not been closed. The plan must be revised and resubmitted on Aconex.

Supervisors and formwork crews had not been briefed on the temporary works procedure, and they were unaware of the need to install structures according to the approved design. The procedure must be communicated to all relevant personnel.
C2.17: No adverse weather working plan had been submitted to the Employer for approval, and there was no defined process for monitoring weather conditions or stopping work. An approved plan is required given the high winds, sandstorms and extreme heat on the project.

The adverse weather plan did not specify wind speed limits for crane operations and work at height, and supervisors were unable to state when work should be stopped. Clear trigger values must be defined and communicated.

The approved plan required weather forecasts to be monitored and communicated daily, but no records of weather monitoring or alerts were available. The contractor must demonstrate that weather information is received and acted upon.

Work at height and lifting continued during high wind conditions, contrary to the stop-work criteria in the approved adverse weather plan. Implementation of the plan must be verified by supervisors on site.

The adverse weather plan was outdated and did not include heat stress management with work-rest cycles, hydration and shaded rest areas. Heat stress controls must be included and implemented during the summer period.

The weather working plan was returned with Code B comments on flash flood and sandstorm response, and the comments had not been addressed. The plan must be revised and approved before the onset of the relevant season.
C2.18: No equipment inspection programme had been submitted for Employer approval, and inspection of plant, tools and equipment was being performed inconsistently. An approved programme is required to define inspection frequencies, colour coding and third-party certification.

Several items of plant were in use without valid third-party inspection certificates, contrary to the approved equipment inspection programme. Equipment without valid certification must be removed from service until inspected.

The colour coding system defined in the approved programme had not been applied, and hand tools and power tools were found without current inspection tags. The contractor must inspect and tag all equipment according to the current period colour.

The equipment inspection programme was outdated and did not include recently mobilised plant such as aerial work platforms and telehandlers. The programme must be updated whenever new equipment arrives on site.

Daily pre-use inspection checklists required by the programme were not completed for cranes and earthmoving equipment, and operators had not been trained on the checklist. Pre-use inspections must be completed and records retained.

The equipment inspection programme was returned with Code C status, and the contractor had not resubmitted a revised programme on Aconex. Equipment inspection was being conducted without an approved programme.
C2.19: No mobilisation and demobilisation plan had been submitted for Employer approval, although new subcontractors and work fronts were being mobilised. An approved plan is required to ensure HSE requirements are met before work starts and when work areas are handed back.

The mobilisation plan did not include a pre-mobilisation HSE checklist covering induction, competency verification, equipment certification and welfare facilities. These elements must be added to ensure readiness before work commences.

Personnel and equipment had been mobilised to a new work area without the readiness review required by the approved plan, and welfare facilities and first aid arrangements were not yet in place. Work must not start until mobilisation requirements are met.

The approved plan was outdated and did not reflect the current project phase, where several work areas were being demobilised. Demobilisation requirements such as removal of temporary services and site restoration must be addressed.
The plan was approved with Code B comments on the handover of demobilised areas, and the comments had not been closed. The plan must be revised and resubmitted for Code A approval.
